Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately. In September 2025 the company's own maintenance team decided to test a shared log in two buildings so that staff on different shifts could see the same information. Eight weeks later, the team had a figure its own trial note does not credit to the software and a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a condition.

## Elm Quay tested repair tracking before picking Svale

In an email interview, maintenance supervisor Maya Lind puts the aim concretely: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done.”

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.

## Elm Quay designed the categories, and Svale built them in

Residents kept the option of reporting repairs by telephone; the team left that route open. Svale Systems configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions, and Lind is precise about the division of work: “The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”

Getting there took longer than Lind expected at one point in particular: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## Trial note records faster assignment but claims no cause

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.

Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. The assessment Lind does give is a qualified one, and it is not drawn from the figures: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

## Expansion waits on a check of larger repairs

The trial has not yet expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs. That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead.

For operations managers weighing a similar trial, [read the implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).

# Elm Quay's trial gives shifts one view of repairs

Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments, tested a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two of its buildings. Its maintenance supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week for preparation – a lesson for any operations manager planning something similar.

By Thomas Barregren

Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately. In September 2025 the company's own maintenance team decided to test a shared log in two buildings so that staff on different shifts could see the same information. Eight weeks later, the team had a figure its own trial note does not credit to the software and a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a condition.

## Elm Quay tested repair tracking before picking Svale

In an email interview, maintenance supervisor Maya Lind puts the aim concretely: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done.”

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.

## Elm Quay designed the categories, and Svale built them in

Residents kept the option of reporting repairs by telephone; the team left that route open. Svale Systems configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions, and Lind is precise about the division of work: “The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”

Getting there took longer than Lind expected at one point in particular: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## Trial note records faster assignment but claims no cause

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.

Nor is assignment the same as completion. There are no measurements of completion time, cost, or resident satisfaction.

## The supervisor would repeat the trial with more preparation

Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. The assessment Lind does give is a qualified one, and it is not drawn from the figures: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

## Expansion waits on a check of larger repairs

The trial has not yet expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs. That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead.

For operations managers weighing a similar trial, [read the implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).
EOF

# Elm Quay's trial gives shifts one view of repairs

Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments, tested a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two of its buildings. Its maintenance supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week for preparation – a lesson for any operations manager planning something similar.

By Thomas Barregren

Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately. In September 2025 the company's own maintenance team decided to test a shared log in two buildings so that staff on different shifts could see the same information. Eight weeks later, the team had a figure its own trial note does not credit to the software and a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a condition.

## Elm Quay tested repair tracking before picking Svale

In an email interview, maintenance supervisor Maya Lind puts the aim concretely: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done.”

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.

## Elm Quay designed the categories, and Svale built them in

Residents kept the option of reporting repairs by telephone; the team left that route open. Svale Systems configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions, and Lind is precise about the division of work: “The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”

Getting there took longer than Lind expected at one point in particular: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## Trial note records faster assignment but claims no cause

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.

Nor is assignment the same as completion. There are no measurements of completion time, cost, or resident satisfaction.

## The supervisor would repeat the trial with more preparation

Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. The assessment Lind does give is a qualified one, and it is not drawn from the figures: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

## Expansion waits on a check of larger repairs

The trial has not yet expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs. That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead.

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

# Claim accounting: draft against supplied material

Draft: `draft.md`. Source: `source.md`. Draft language en_US, source English, quotations not translated. So there are no translation findings, and every finding below is a source-support finding. The byline is excluded, as instructed.

## A. Claim-by-claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage (D), the source passage (S) and the comparison.

**A1. Title.** D: "Elm Quay's repair trial gives shifts one view".
S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information." and Lind: "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done." and "Having one view of the reports helps us".
Difference: the source gives shifts sharing information only as the team's aim. It shows that one view exists only through Lind's "one view of the reports helps us", where "us" means the team, not the shifts. The title turns the aim into an achieved result for the shifts. See **F1**.

**A2. Dek, sentence 1.** D: "Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments, tested a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two of its buildings."
S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings." and "It chose Svale Systems".
Difference: "flats" and "apartments" name the same thing in en_US. "Its buildings" means buildings that Elm Quay manages. Nothing in this context separates managing from owning in a way that changes the claim. Supported.

**A3. Dek, sentence 2, first part.** D: "Its maintenance supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week for preparation".
S: "I would choose to do the trial again. … but I would leave an extra week for preparation." and "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind".
Difference: none of substance. The conditional "would" is kept, and the extra week is stated. Supported.

**A4. Dek, sentence 2, second part.** D: "—a lesson for any operations manager planning something similar."
S: no source passage. The draft generalises Lind's own intention ("I would leave an extra week").
Assessment: this is the author's framing, resting on a supported quotation. It concerns preparation time, not a recommendation of Svale, so it does not contradict "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company." It is not a defect. It is an **editorial question (E1)**: "any" presents Lind's personal plan as general advice, which the material does not give as anybody's position.

**A5. Paragraph 1, sentence 1.** D: "Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately."
S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately." and "kept telephone reporting open for residents."
Difference: in the source, "previously" applies only to the separate storage. In the draft, "used to" also governs the arrival channels, which implies that reports no longer arrive by telephone. The source says telephone reporting stayed open. See **F2**.

- (a) The pronoun "its" is third-person singular and non-personal, referring to "the team". "Its own trial note" therefore makes the maintenance team the owner or author of the note. The source says only "Elm Quay's internal trial note". See **F3**.

Difference: none. The first sentence is the author's clarification and makes no factual claim. Supported.
